title: AGI Is a Marathon: Physical Hardware Has Become the Biggest Bottleneck
dek: Last year we thought adding GPUs and data would get us to AGI; this year we find that a single data center hits a wall at 32,000 cards, and US energy infrastructure was planned forty or fifty years ago—the AGI timeline has been stretched out by the physical world.
why: A frontline investor strings compute, energy, models, products, and alliances into one AGI infrastructure map, dense with numbers, suited for anyone who wants to quickly calibrate their judgment.
who: Founders, investors, and engineers following AGI progress, who want to use one episode to calibrate their judgment on compute, energy, models, and products.
skip: The chat about carbon-based and silicon-based life after 1:15:47 can be skipped.

points.h: AGI has gone from a sprint to a marathon
points.body: Early last year everyone thought AGI was a hundred-meter sprint and no one was prepared; this year it has become a marathon, and everyone has ample time to prepare. The change comes from a concrete discovery: last year we thought we could add GPUs and data indefinitely to reach AGI, but suddenly we found that GPU data centers and physical hardware are a huge bottleneck—a single data center now scales to 32,000 cards, and going beyond that requires breaking through many limits; US energy infrastructure was planned forty or fifty years ago, and the energy mix is vastly different, so suddenly adding a lot of electricity demand really can't keep up. So the biggest feeling this year is that physical hardware has become the biggest factor hindering the AGI timeline.

points.h: The economy and society suddenly got two new taxes
points.body: One judgment is: model companies may be where value accumulates most thickly, just as mobile internet value accumulated in device makers and advertising platforms. Thus two taxes appear—Jensen Huang's GPUs collect a compute tax, and models collect an intelligence tax, suddenly adding two taxes to the economy and society. But Li Guangmi also gives the counterargument: if large models are electricity, the light bulb isn't necessarily made by the power plant. He leans toward large model companies being a research lab for basic discoveries; some labs have commercial capability and will produce top applications, but that tests organizational capability.

points.h: GPT-4's ticket price is 300 million dollars
points.body: Break training cost into electricity and cards: assume GPT-3.5 trains on 500 H100s for 15 days, about 250,000 kWh, which is 0.05% of the Three Gorges or Shanghai's electricity consumption; GPT-4 trains on 8,000 H100s for 100 days, about 26 million kWh, which is 5% of the Three Gorges or Shanghai's daily electricity consumption, and 2% of Texas's; if GPT-5 trains on 32,000 H100s for 100 days, it's about 20% of the Three Gorges or Shanghai's daily electricity consumption. In money: each H100 sells for $30,000, plus peripheral equipment, 8,000 cards is over $300 million—$300 million is the ticket price for GPT-4; a 32,000-card cluster means $1.2 to $1.3 billion.

points.h: The bottleneck for a 10,000-card cluster isn't money
points.body: A 10,000-card cluster is standard, but money alone isn't enough. Every card must be connected, interconnection is very difficult, and the network topology isn't one layer but three. Factors affecting difficulty include: finding land suitable for a GPU data center, stable and cheap electricity, interconnection and communication of data centers, and the reliability of cooling and operations. Resources are increasingly concentrated and converging; few customers can build large clusters, and it will converge to only four or five major customers. Things in the physical world are slower to transform than the digital world.

points.h: Scaling Law hasn't slowed; compute just hasn't been pushed enough
points.body: GPT-4 publicly has 1.8T parameters, MOE architecture, about 13T data, trained on 25,000 A100s for 100 days. Assume the next generation has triple parameters and triple data, that's 9x compute; Jensen Huang's announced 32,000 H100 cluster plus optimization efficiency gains just matches; wanting 10x parameters and 10x data is 100x compute, clearly not enough. The conclusion is that Scaling Law hasn't slowed; if it seems slower, it's that compute and data haven't been pushed enough—GPT-3.5 to GPT-4 used roughly twenty to thirty times compute increase, and from GPT-4 to the next generation we haven't yet pushed enough twenty to thirty times effective compute.

points.h: This year you must surpass GPT-4, or you're out
points.body: 2024 is the year of convergence for large model companies. The technical life-or-death line is that within this year you must surpass GPT-4, which requires a very strong team behind it; second- and third-tier model companies, including domestic ones, must surpass the best open-source models, otherwise their commercial value is relatively small. On compute, this year you must use a 10,000-card cluster, and companies that can do a 10,000-card cluster well are still relatively few. The next 12 months will show whether a 100,000 H100 cluster is possible, roughly $3-5 billion investment. Globally, the ones that can remain: in the US possibly OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Musk's xAI—four companies; in Europe Mistral is good but it's uncertain whether Europe is an independent market.

points.h: OpenAI doing products is forced by circumstances
points.body: There are three new understandings of OpenAI: the AGI timeline may be stretched; an AGI company shouldn't be too aggressive with products at first, but OpenAI is now very aggressive; and starting to understand gradual unlocking. Why aggressively do applications? Li Guangmi guesses: if AGI takes 10 years, each year requires several billion or even 10 billion dollars of investment, so commercialization is needed, and sustained healthy cash flow is needed to support AGI; relying purely on financing it's hard to raise that much money, and you can't just depend on Microsoft. He also judges that OpenAI is harder on the 2B enterprise side, because enterprise customers care about trust, and Microsoft is too deeply trusted by enterprise customers, so a large part of OpenAI's 2B value may be taken by Microsoft.

points.h: Silicon Valley VC's three big things: coding, agent, robotics
points.body: Silicon Valley VC's investment theme this year is three big things: coding, agent, and robotics. But Li Guangmi is skeptical of all three: coding is certainly within the core range of large model companies and Microsoft, the core capability comes from model companies, these coding startups won't train their own large models, and it's uncertain how much value the optimization layer on top has; model companies may be very aggressive in doing agents, because the added value is high, it's model-level capability, model-level application, model-level agent. He leans toward short-term value still accumulating in the models themselves. Robotics is the first choice for many researcher startups, because it's easier to tell a story.
